title: Live Oaks Over a Houston Roof
description: A live oak shades a Houston house and scrapes the shingles in the wind. Trim limbs clear of the roof before the next storm drops one through the deck.
html:
The tree is why the house stays cooler, and it is also why the roof stays damp, full of leaves, and one wind event away from a hole. Live oaks around Houston do not need to be cut down to save a roof. They do need enough air between the limbs and the shingles that the tree and the roof are not sanding each other.

What the limbs actually do

A branch that rests on the roof, or swings into it, scrapes granules off in a patch you can outline. That bald spot ages faster than the field. Leaves and catkins fill the valleys and the gutter. Water that should have run to the downspout sits, and the ceiling stain shows up at an inside corner. Shade on the north slope feeds the dark streaks. None of that is a reason to remove a healthy oak. It is a reason to prune with a clearance in mind, and to clean the valleys on a schedule instead of after the stain.

A falling limb is the other problem. Small deadwood punches a hole the size of the branch. A lead from the trunk can break rafters, and that is no longer a roofing-only repair. After a storm, look for holes and cracked deck, not just branches lying in the yard. A hole gets a tarp the same day. A scrape can wait for a calmer look.

Who cuts, and who roofs

We do not take down live oaks. An arborist who knows this tree should do the pruning, including how much canopy an oak can lose in a year without being harmed. We will point at the limbs that are in the roof and the ones that are only shading it. After the cut, we repair the punctures, the scraped courses, and the valleys the leaves dammed.

If the oak is already on the shingles, start with a roof inspection so you know whether you are buying pruning, a repair, or both. Storm tarping is the call when a limb is through the deck tonight. Otherwise call (281) 541-0027 or request a free inspection.
